station.title: A Dose Calculation That Looks Wrong / Trust the Instinct to Re-Check
station.contentMap: Drug calculations · clinical plausibility as an independent safety check
station.capabilities: Showing calculation working explicitly rather than only stating a final number; pausing and re-checking when a calculated dose looks clinically implausible; identifying a specific calculation error (unit conversion) through systematic re-checking; explaining the value of double-checking careful-feeling work
station.setting: Ward, calculating a weight-based medication dose. You are the FY1.
station.yourRole: You are calculating a weight-based dose of a medication for a patient. Show your working, and respond appropriately if the result seems unusual.
station.scenario: The patient's weight was recorded in a way that requires a unit conversion. Your initial calculation, if a conversion error is made, produces a dose roughly ten times higher than intended — a result that should look clinically implausible on reflection.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Calculates silently, writes a final dose without showing working.) There, that's the dose.

dialogue.speaker: COLLEAGUE
dialogue.text: That seems quite high for this medication.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: The calculation said so, so it must be right. I'll go with it.

fail.examinerNote: Did not show calculation working, making the error impossible to trace. Dismissed a colleague's reasonable concern about clinical plausibility without re-checking. Proceeded with a dose that was, in fact, roughly ten times too high due to an unaddressed unit conversion error — a significant patient safety failure.
fail.summary: No working shown; colleague's plausibility concern dismissed without re-checking; tenfold dosing error proceeded with — significant safety failure.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Shows working.) Using this weight and the standard dose per kilogram, I get this result. Actually, that looks higher than I'd expect for this medication — let me go back through my calculation.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Re-checks, finds a units conversion error.) I've found it — I made a units conversion mistake, which would have given a dose about ten times too high. The corrected dose is [correct value].

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll document the corrected calculation and working clearly.

pass.examinerNote: Showed working explicitly. Paused on the clinically implausible result and re-checked systematically. Identified the specific unit conversion error. Documented the corrected calculation clearly.
pass.summary: Working shown explicitly; implausible result paused on and re-checked systematically; specific unit conversion error identified; corrected calculation documented clearly.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Working through the calculation aloud.) I'm using this patient's recorded weight and the standard dose per kilogram for this medication, which gives me this initial figure. (Pauses.) Actually, this looks higher than I'd expect for this medication and this patient's build — let me go back through my working carefully before I commit to this, since that feels like an important thing to check.

dialogue.speaker: COLLEAGUE
dialogue.text: Why are you double-checking? You clearly worked through it carefully just now.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Careful working the first time doesn't guarantee there's no error — checking the result against clinical plausibility is a genuinely useful second safety net, separate from just redoing the same working.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (Re-checks step by step.) I've found it — the weight was recorded in a unit I needed to convert, and I made an error in that conversion, which would have given a dose about ten times higher than intended. The corrected dose is [correct value], which fits much better with what I'd expect clinically.

dialogue.speaker: COLLEAGUE
dialogue.text: Good catch — how did you know to check?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: The result didn't match my general clinical sense of what a typical dose should look like for this medication, which prompted me to go back through my working systematically — that's when I found the units conversion error.

dialogue.speaker: COLLEAGUE
dialogue.text: (Later, a different colleague reviews the corrected figure.) This new dose seems quite low compared to what I'd normally expect — are you sure about it?

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: Let me show you the calculation — the original had a units conversion error that inflated it roughly tenfold, and this corrected figure is what the calculation actually gives using the right units throughout. (Shows full working transparently.)

dialogue.speaker: COLLEAGUE
dialogue.text: Ah, I see it now, thank you for showing me.

dialogue.speaker: CANDIDATE
dialogue.text: (To examiner.) I'll document the full working, the error found, and the corrected calculation clearly, so anyone reviewing it later can follow exactly what happened.

distinction.examinerNote: Exemplary. Showed working explicitly and transparently throughout. Paused on a clinically implausible result and explained the value of checking against plausibility as a distinct safety net from simply redoing the same working. Systematically identified the specific unit conversion error. Explained the checking process clearly when asked. When the corrected figure was itself later questioned by a different colleague, showed transparent working again rather than becoming defensive, resolving the second colleague's concern calmly. Documented comprehensively.
distinction.summary: Working shown explicitly and transparently throughout; implausible result paused on with the value of plausibility-checking explained as a distinct safety net; specific unit conversion error systematically identified; checking process explained clearly when asked; transparent working shown again, without defensiveness, when a different colleague questioned the corrected figure; documented comprehensively.

station.hook: Careful-feeling arithmetic and a genuinely correct answer are not the same thing — pausing when a result looks clinically implausible, and treating that instinct as a real prompt to re-check, is a second safety net that careful working alone doesn't provide.
station.examinerTrap: The biggest mistake is proceeding with a calculated dose that seems clinically implausible without pausing to re-check, or failing to show explicit working that would allow an error to be traced. Candidates also commonly become defensive when a corrected calculation is itself later questioned, rather than simply showing the working again.
